title: Sustainability and Carbon Accounting
answer: Emissions data, claims checking, combined reporting, disclosure drafting and carbon credit records.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Collecting Emissions Data
children.blurb: Collecting emissions data covers the gathering of greenhouse gas figures across Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3, from fuel bills and meter readings through to supplier reports and spend records.

children.name: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
children.blurb: Checking claims against the ledger is the practice of testing a stated emissions or sustainability figure against the underlying records that are supposed to support it.

children.name: Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data
children.blurb: Combining financial and non-financial data means bringing together figures from the general ledger, such as spend, revenue and cost, with measures that never appear in it, such as emissions, energy use, headcount, water draw or supplier ratings.

children.name: Drafting Sustainability Disclosures
children.blurb: Drafting sustainability disclosures covers the preparation of climate and environmental reporting that companies publish for regulators, investors and the public.

children.name: Carbon Credit Records
children.blurb: Carbon credit records are the documented trail of a unit of greenhouse gas reduction or removal, from the project that generated it through verification, issuance, transfer and retirement.

sections.body: Sustainability and carbon accounting is the work of measuring what an organisation emits, verifying what it says about those emissions, and reporting both in a form that auditors, regulators and investors can follow. Artificial intelligence is being used on the messy front end of this work, pulling figures out of utility bills, fuel receipts, shipping records and supplier questionnaires and turning them into structured entries. It is also used to scan narrative claims in reports and press releases against the underlying transaction data, flagging statements that the numbers do not support. Language models help draft disclosure text from the same structured data, and classification models sort carbon credit holdings by type, vintage and retirement status. The point is not to replace the accountant or the assurance provider, it is to cut the manual reconciliation that makes sustainability reporting slow and error prone.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Emissions data collection is the most mature part, because extraction from invoices and meter readings is a well understood document task and the outputs can be checked against source files. Claims checking is harder, since it depends on whether the ledger is complete in the first place, and a claim can be technically true while resting on a boundary the company chose for itself. Combining financial and non financial data runs into the fact that the two are kept on different systems, different calendars and different definitions of a reporting entity, so mapping is often bespoke. Disclosure drafting works best as a first pass that a human rewrites, because frameworks change and the model has no reliable sense of which version applies. Carbon credit records remain the weakest area, since registry data is fragmented, credits are not fungible, and questions of ownership and retirement are legal matters rather than pattern matching problems. Nothing here removes the need for assurance, and no model output should be treated as a verified figure on its own.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages follow the reporting chain from raw data to published claim. Collecting Emissions Data covers the extraction and structuring step, which is where most of the practical value currently sits. Checking Claims Against the Ledger takes those structured figures and tests the statements built on them, so it is the page to read when the question is whether a number in a report can be traced back to a source. Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data deals with the join between the two systems, the part that decides whether a sustainability figure can sit beside a financial one in the same statement. Drafting Sustainability Disclosures is about turning the reconciled data into text, and it depends on everything upstream being sound. Carbon Credit Records stands slightly apart, covering the tracking of credits and their retirement, and a reader should treat it as the least settled of the five.
